{{short description|Given a triangle and a point, constructs a second triangle with a special point}}
[[File:Maxwell theorem2.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Line segments with identical markings are parallel.<br/> If the sides of the triangle<math>A'B'C'</math> are parallel to the according cevians of triangle <math>ABC</math>, which are  intersecting in a common point <math>V'</math>, then the cevians of triangle <math>A'B'C'</math>, which are parallel to the according sides of triangle <math>ABC</math> intersect in a common point <math>V'</math> as well]]
'''Maxwell's theorem''' is the following statement about triangles in the plane.

{{quote|For a given triangle <math>ABC</math> and a point <math>V</math> not on the sides of that triangle construct a second triangle <math>A'B'C'</math>, such that the side <math>A'B'</math> is parallel to the line segment <math>CV</math>, the side <math>A'C'</math> is parallel to the line segment <math>BV</math> and the side <math>B'C'</math> is parallel to the line segment <math>AV</math>. Then the parallel to <math>AB</math> through <math>C'</math>, the parallel to <math>BC</math> through <math>A'</math> and the parallel to <math>AC</math> through <math>B'</math> intersect in a common point <math>V'</math>.}}

The theorem is named after the physicist [[James Clerk Maxwell]] (1831–1879), who proved it in his work on [[reciprocal figures]], which are of importance in [[statics]].
